# Obsessive-compulsive disorder

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Psychiatry > Anxiety disorders > Obsessive-compulsive disorder*

[Original Article Link](/library/OP0IUT)

---

## Summary

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (<u>OCD</u>) is characterized by recurrent thoughts or urges (i.e., <u>obsessions</u>) that often lead to repetitive behaviors or mental acts (i.e., <u>compulsions</u>). <u>Obsessions</u> are experienced as intrusive, involuntary, and undesirable, and they generally cause <u>anxiety</u> and/or <u>distress</u>. While <u>compulsions</u> are not generally experienced as pleasurable, their performance may provide relief from the <u>distress</u> and <u>anxiety</u> caused by an <u>obsession</u>. <u>Compulsions</u> and <u>obsessions</u> are uncontrollable and time-consuming, leading to significant function impairment. Comorbidity with other psychiatric disorders (e.g., <u>anxiety disorders</u>, <u>mood disorders</u>, <u>tic disorders</u>) is common. Treatment includes <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u> (<u>CBT</u>) and/or <u>selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors</u> (<u>SSRIs</u>).

---

## Etiology

The etiology of <u>OCD</u> is multifactorial. Factors that have been associated with <u>OCD</u> development include:




* Genetic: familial transmission

* Neurobiological: abnormalities in the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuit, including the orbitofrontal cortex, <u>anterior</u> cingulate cortex, and <u>striatum</u>

* <u>Serotonin</u> level imbalance may play a role.

* Infection: pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with <u>streptococcal</u> infections (<u>PANDAS</u>)

* Psychological trauma

---

## Clinical features

### Symptoms [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)[[3]](/library/0hdecp0)




Behavior and thought patterns of <u>OCD</u> are <u>egodystonic</u> (i.e., inconsistent with or repulsive to one's sense of self).




* Obsessions (recurrent, intrusive, and distressing thoughts or urges), e.g.:

* Fears around contamination of self and/or others

* Worries about immorality

* Fixation on symmetry and order

* Fear of harming self and/or others

* Compulsions (repetitive behaviors or mental acts to provide relief from <u>anxiety</u> caused by <u>obsessions</u>; can be substantially time-consuming), e.g.:

* Excessive cleaning or hand-washing

* Repetitive “neutralizing” thoughts or prayers

* Ordering and rearranging objects

* Checking that tasks have been done correctly, e.g., opening and closing a door multiple times to confirm it is locked

* <u>Obsessions</u> and <u>compulsions</u> can lead to severe <u>anxiety</u> and avoidance behaviors (e.g., avoiding situations that may trigger symptoms).





> [!NOTE]
> Unlike individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder, individuals with <u>obsessive-compulsive personality disorder</u> show <u>egosyntonic</u> behavior.




### Comorbidities [[4]](/library/Yhdncp0)




Most individuals with <u>OCD</u> have comorbid psychiatric disorders, e.g.:




* <u>Anxiety disorders</u>

* <u>Mood disorders</u>, e.g., <u>depressive disorders</u>, <u>bipolar disorder</u>

* <u>Impulse control disorders</u>

* <u>Tic disorders</u>, e.g., <u>Tourette syndrome</u>

* <u>Personality disorders</u>

* <u>Schizophrenia</u> or <u>schizoaffective disorder</u>

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[3]](/library/0hdecp0)




* Consider screening tools, e.g., the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) in patients with <u>symptoms of OCD</u>.  [[3]](/library/0hdecp0)

* Rule out <u>differential diagnoses of OCD</u> and assess for comorbidites (e.g., <u>anxiety</u> and <u>mood disorders</u>).

* Confirm the diagnosis using the <u>DSM-5 TR</u> diagnostic criteria for <u>OCD</u>.

* <u>Evaluate suicide risk</u>.





### <u>DSM-5 TR</u> diagnostic criteria for <u>OCD</u> [[2]](/library/muWV7M0)[[3]](/library/0hdecp0)[[5]](/library/ahdQcp0)




#### Diagnostic criteria




Diagnosis is confirmed in individuals who meet all of the following criteria.




* Presence of <u>obsessions</u> and/or <u>compulsions</u>

* <u>Obsessions</u> are defined by both of the following:

* Recurrent, intrusive, and distressing thoughts or urges

* Attempts to suppress or neutralize these thoughts or urges

* <u>Compulsions</u> are defined by both of the following:

* Repetitive behaviors or mental acts that the individual feels compelled to do to relieve <u>anxiety</u> brought upon by <u>obsessions</u>

* When behaviors or mental actions are performed to prevent an unwanted event, they are excessive or cannot be realistically connected to the event.

* Symptoms are time-consuming (e.g., ≥ 1 hour/day) and/or result in significant <u>distress</u> or impairment;  in key areas of functioning (e.g., school, work, social life).

* Symptoms are not attributable to:

* The effects of a substance or medication

* Another medical or psychiatric condition (See “Differential diagnoses of obsessive-compulsive disorder.”)





#### Specifiers




Specifiers provide additional information on the diagnosis, which can be used to support management decisions.




* Level of insight: the patient's degree of understanding that their thoughts are not true  [[3]](/library/0hdecp0)[[5]](/library/ahdQcp0)

* <u>Tic</u>-related <u>OCD</u>: current or past diagnosis of a <u>tic disorder</u>  [[3]](/library/0hdecp0)

---

## Differential diagnoses

| <u>Differential diagnoses of OCD</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Characteristics |
| Obsessive compulsive disorder |  | <br><br>* <u>Intrusive thoughts</u>, images, and urges that trigger repetitive, <u>compulsive behavior</u><br><br>* <u>Egodystonic</u>: behavior patterns are not in agreement with ideal self-image<br><br><br> |
| <u>Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder</u> |  | <br><br>* Excessive perfectionism and rigid control regarding real-life concerns<br><br>* Behavior is <u>egosyntonic</u>, meaning that the affected individual's thought and behavior patterns are congruent with their self-image and therefore they do not perceive them as wrong.<br><br><br> |
| <u>OCD-related disorders</u> | <u>Excoriation disorder</u> | <br>* Recurrent <u>skin</u> picking resulting in lesions<br><br> |
| <u>Hoarding disorder</u> | <br>* Difficulty discarding belongings<br><br> |  |
| <u>Body dysmorphic disorder</u> | <br>* <u>Obsessions</u> and <u>compulsions</u> revolve around physical appearance.<br><br> |  |
| <u>Trichotillomania</u> | <br>* <u>Compulsive behavior</u> is limited to <u>hair</u> pulling in the absence of <u>obsessions</u>.<br><br> |  |
| <u>Tic disorder</u> |  | <br>* <u>Tics</u> are involuntary, not responses to <u>obsessions</u> and/or <u>compulsions</u>.<br><br> |
| <u>Generalized anxiety disorder</u> |  | <br>* Recurrent thoughts revolve around real-life concerns, e.g., work, as opposed to the <u>obsessions</u> in <u>OCD</u>, which tend to be of an irrational nature.<br><br> |
| <u>Major depressive disorder</u> |  | <br>* Recurrent thoughts are typically about past events, are not usually experienced as intrusive, and often revolve around negative thoughts, e.g., guilt.<br><br> |




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## OCD-related disorders

### Excoriation disorder [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)[[2]](/library/muWV7M0)




* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>

* Onset: <u>adolescence</u>

* Comorbidities: <u>OCD</u>, <u>trichotillomania</u>, <u>MDD</u>, BDD

* Diagnostic criteria (<u>DSM-5 TR</u>) [[2]](/library/muWV7M0)

* Recurrent <u>skin</u> picking resulting in lesions

* Repeated attempts to decrease or stop picking

* Symptoms cause significant <u>distress</u> or impairment in daily functioning

* Not due to any substance disorder or another medical or psychiatric disorder (e.g., <u>tactile hallucinations</u>, intentional self-harm, BDD, <u>eczema</u>, <u>psoriasis</u>, <u>scabies</u>)

* Treatment

* <u>Habit reversal therapy</u>

* Evidence for pharmacological treatment is limited. [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)





### Hoarding disorder [[6]](/library/RuWlIM0)




* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>Point prevalence</u>: ∼ 2–6%

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[6]](/library/RuWlIM0)

* Diagnostic criteria (<u>DSM-5 TR</u>) [[6]](/library/RuWlIM0)

* Persistent urge to keep belongings

* Difficulty discarding belongings, regardless of their value

* Accumulation of belongings, which causes the intended use of belongings to be compromised and living areas to be cluttered.

* Not explained by other medical conditions (e.g., <u>brain</u> injuries) or mental illness (e.g., <u>OCD</u>)

* Results in significant <u>distress</u>/impairment in key areas of functioning (work, social life)

* Not due to another medical condition (e.g., <u>brain injury</u>) or psychiatric disorder (e.g., <u>OCD</u>)

* Treatment [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)

* <u>CBT</u>

* There is currently no evidence of pharmacological treatment <u>efficacy</u>.





### Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) [[2]](/library/muWV7M0)




* Definition: an excessive preoccupation with perceived flaws or defects in appearance

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>Prevalence</u>: ∼ 2.5% [[2]](/library/muWV7M0)

* <u>♂</u> ≈ <u>♀</u>  [[2]](/library/muWV7M0)

* Mean age of onset: 17 years [[2]](/library/muWV7M0)

* Diagnostic criteria (<u>DSM-5 TR</u>) [[2]](/library/muWV7M0)

* Persistent preoccupation with one or more perceived flaws in physical appearance that are mild or imperceivable to others

* Repetitive behaviors (e.g., constantly checking the mirror, <u>skin</u> picking, excessive grooming) or thoughts about one's appearance (e.g., comparing oneself to others)

* Results in significant <u>distress</u> and impairment in key areas of functioning (e.g., school, work, social life)

* Symptoms are not due to an <u>eating disorder</u>.

* Specifiers

* Muscle dysmorphia: a preoccupation with one's body not being muscular, large, or lean enough

* Occurs almost exclusively in men

* Affected individuals may use <u>anabolic steroids</u> or other potentially dangerous substances to increase muscle mass.

* Level of insight

* Absent insight or <u>delusional</u> beliefs: Patients perceive their beliefs as true.

* Poor insight: Patients perceive their beliefs as probably true.

* Good insight: Patients perceive their beliefs as definitely/probably false.

* Treatment [[7]](/library/OQdIwp0)

* First-line treatment: <u>SSRIs</u> and/or <u>CBT</u> [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)

* General measures

* Educate patients about BDD and available treatment options.

* Avoid making remarks (positive or negative) on the patient's appearance, challenging their beliefs, or dismissing their perceived flaw as minor and/or imagined. [[7]](/library/OQdIwp0)

* Consider involving family members, if appropriate.

* Cosmetic interventions are not recommended in patients with BDD.  [[7]](/library/OQdIwp0)





### Trichotillomania (<u>hair-pulling disorder</u>) [[6]](/library/RuWlIM0)




* Definition: an irresistible <u>compulsion</u> to pull out one's <u>hair</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>Prevalence</u>: ∼ 2% [[6]](/library/RuWlIM0)

* <u>♀</u> 10:1 <u>♂</u> [[6]](/library/RuWlIM0)

* Onset is usually in <u>adolescence</u> following a stressful event but can happen at any age.

* Comorbidities (e.g., <u>MDD</u>, <u>excoriation disorder</u>) are common.

* Clinical features

* <u>Hair</u> loss, most commonly involving the scalp, eyebrows, or eyelashes

* The pattern of <u>hair</u> loss is usually patchy, with <u>hair</u> of different lengths.

* Diagnostic criteria (<u>DSM-5 TR</u>) [[6]](/library/RuWlIM0)

* <u>Hair</u> loss due to recurrent pulling out of one's <u>hair</u>

* Repeated attempts to ; decrease or stop this behavior

* Results in significant <u>distress</u>/impairment in key areas of functioning (e.g., school, work, social life)

* Not due to another medical condition (e.g., <u>skin</u> disease) or psychiatric disorder (e.g., <u>body dysmorphic disorder</u>)

* Differential diagnosis: <u>alopecia</u>

* Treatment [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)

* <u>CBT</u>: <u>habit reversal therapy</u>

* Limited evidence for <u>SSRIs</u>

## Treatment

### Approach [[3]](/library/0hdecp0)[[5]](/library/ahdQcp0)




* First-line treatments: <u>CBT</u> and/or <u>SSRIs</u>

* Consider <u>psychiatry</u> referral for patients with any of the following: [[3]](/library/0hdecp0)

* Severe <u>OCD symptoms</u>

* Poor insight

* Significant comorbidities (e.g., <u>tic disorders</u>, <u>hoarding disorders</u>, <u>MDD</u>)

* Inadequate response to <u>SSRIs</u>

* Treat comorbidities (e.g., <u>MDD</u>, <u>anxiety disorders</u>).

* Consider hospitalization for patients with <u>suicidal ideation</u> or who are unable to adequately care for themselves. [[5]](/library/ahdQcp0)

* See “Special patient groups” for <u>OCD in children</u> and <u>OCD in pregnant and postpartum individuals</u>.





### <u>Cognitive behavioral therapy</u> [[3]](/library/0hdecp0)[[4]](/library/Yhdncp0)




* Monotherapy: patients with mild to moderate symptoms or when <u>SSRIs</u> are contraindicated (e.g., comorbid <u>bipolar disorder</u>, <u>pregnancy</u>)

* <u>CBT</u> with <u>SSRIs</u>: patients with inadequate response to <u>CBT</u> or <u>SSRI</u> as monotherapy or for severe symptoms  [[4]](/library/Yhdncp0)

* Recommended therapy modalities include <u>cognitive therapy</u> and <u>exposure and response prevention</u>.





### Pharmacological treatment [[4]](/library/Yhdncp0)




* <u>SSRIs</u>, e.g., <u>sertraline</u> DOSAGE, <u>paroxetine</u> DOSAGE, <u>fluoxetine</u> DOSAGE, <u>fluvoxamine</u> DOSAGE

* In combination with <u>CBT</u>, e.g., in patients with severe symptoms

* As monotherapy, e.g., if <u>CBT</u> is not available or declined

* Refractory <u>OCD</u>

* Combination of <u>CBT</u> and an <u>SSRI</u> if initial treatment was monotherapy

* Consider switching to one of the following:

* A different <u>SSRI</u>

* A <u>tricyclic antidepressant</u> with serotonergic action, e.g., <u>clomipramine</u>   [[3]](/library/0hdecp0)

* An <u>SNRI</u>, e.g., <u>venlafaxine</u> (<u>off-label</u>) [[5]](/library/ahdQcp0)

* A combination of an <u>antipsychotic</u> agent (<u>off-label</u>), e.g., <u>risperidone</u>, <u>quetiapine</u>, and an <u>SSRI</u> may be considered. [[3]](/library/0hdecp0)

## Special patient groups

### OCD in children [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)




* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>Prevalence</u> 1–2 % [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)

* Psychiatric comorbidities are common.

* Diagnostics

* See “<u>Diagnostics for OCD</u>.”

* In patients with abrupt onset, <u>PANDAS</u> may be considered.

* Management

* Mild or moderate symptoms: <u>CBT</u> with <u>exposure and response prevention therapy</u>

* Severe symptoms: <u>CBT</u> and <u>SSRIs</u>, e.g., <u>sertraline</u> DOSAGE, <u>fluvoxamine</u> DOSAGE





### OCD in pregnant and postpartum individuals




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: New-onset <u>OCD</u> occurs in up to 22% of pregnant individuals. [[8]](/library/9hdNTp0)

* Clinical features

* See “<u>Clinical features of OCD</u>.”

* Pregnant and postpartum individuals may show particular <u>obsessions</u> and <u>compulsions</u>.





| Common <u>obsessions</u> and <u>compulsions</u> in pregnant and postpartum individuals |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Examples of <u>obsessions</u> | Examples of resulting <u>compulsions</u> |
| During <u>pregnancy</u> | <br>* Fetal <u>death</u><br><br> | <br>* Repeated provocation of fetal movement (e.g., poking the belly) to ensure the fetus is still alive<br><br> |
| <br>* Contamination of the fetus (e.g., by bacteria) [[8]](/library/9hdNTp0)<br><br> | <br>* Excessive washing and cleaning<br><br> |  |
| <br>* Aggressive <u>obsession</u> symptoms relating to the fetus (i.e., persistent thoughts of being responsible for harm to the fetus, whether intentional or not)<br><br> | <br><br>* Hiding all objects that might be used to harm the fetus<br><br>* Avoiding driving for fear of an accident<br><br><br> |  |
| Postpartum | <br>* <u>Sudden infant death syndrome</u><br><br> | <br>* Repeated checking on the <u>infant</u> (esp. at night) [[8]](/library/9hdNTp0)<br><br> |
| <br>* Fear of malpositioning the baby<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Contaminating the <u>infant</u> [[8]](/library/9hdNTp0)<br><br> | <br>* Excessive washing and cleaning of the <u>infant</u> and <u>infant</u> equipment [[8]](/library/9hdNTp0)<br><br> |  |
| <br>* Aggressive <u>obsession</u> symptoms relating to the <u>infant</u> (i.e., persistent thoughts of being responsible for harm to the <u>infant</u>, whether intentional or not, incl. intrusive sexual thoughts) [[8]](/library/9hdNTp0)<br><br> | <br>* Avoidance of being alone with the <u>infant</u> or changing diapers<br><br> |  |
| <br>* Poor parenting skills or criticism of parenting skills from others<br><br> | <br><br>* Excessive research on the topic of parenting<br><br>* Avoiding parenting groups due to fear of criticism<br><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Intrusive thoughts</u> of <u>infant</u> harm in postpartum <u>OCD</u> are <u>egodystonic</u> and often shocking to the parent, whereas <u>egosyntonic</u> thoughts about harming an <u>infant</u> may indicate <u>postpartum psychosis</u>. [[8]](/library/9hdNTp0)




> [!WARNING]
> Patients with <u>perinatal</u> <u>OCD</u> are not at risk of intentionally harming their child, but patients with <u>postpartum psychosis</u> may be because of <u>delusional</u> beliefs. [[8]](/library/9hdNTp0)




* Diagnostics

* See “<u>Diagnostics for obsessive-compulsive disorder</u>.”

* Rule out other <u>perinatal</u> psychiatric disorders, especially <u>postpartum psychosis</u>.

* Management [[8]](/library/9hdNTp0)

* Consult <u>psychiatry</u>. [[9]](/library/WMWPnN0)

* Management is similar to non-pregnant individuals. See also “Treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder” above.

* First-line treatment: <u>CBT</u>: <u>exposure and response prevention therapy</u> [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)

* <u>SSRIs</u> (e.g., <u>sertraline</u>) may be considered with or without <u>CBT</u> in moderate or severe symptoms, or if response to <u>CBT</u> monotherapy is inadequate.

* Offer other supportive measures, e.g., <u>family therapy</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Pharmacotherapy during pregnancy</u> and <u>breastfeeding</u> should only be given after weighing risks and benefits under specialist guidance. [[1]](/library/ySddXp0)[[4]](/library/Yhdncp0)
